meaningMnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means belt .

Who wears cleats and takes your measurements for so long that icicles start forming on your body? Your commander . The commander is very, very particular. And everyone knows the commander has to get everything exactly right. So taking your measurements takes SO long that icicles grow out of your nose. But that's okay. You have to impress your new commander, darn it!

This radical looks like a big, weird caterpillar bug thing. But, for the sake of everyone's sanity, we'll just call it sake , okay? Keep in mind, we mean sake as in "for the sake of X," not as in the alcoholic beverage!
See the shuriken stuck in the ground? In case you don't know, a shuriken is just a throwing star — that thing ninjas use. This looks just like one, right? That's why it's the shuriken radical.

This is the turtle radical. You can tell because there's a big shell in the middle, a whole head on top, and a tail at the bottom. You probably could have guessed this was a turtle without me even telling you, it's so turtle-like.

The ability to boil is one of the main abilities of a bear . Hints I bet you didn't know this, but a bear can boil whenever it wants. Imagine a bear heating itself up and boiling, its fur and skin bubbling and letting off steam.
readingMnemonic: A bear boiling in front of you should fill you with great honor. Or, as they say in Latin: Magna cum ( くま ) laude. Get it? A little hot bear humor for you. Hints You can also imagine a bear graduating in the top 5-10% of its class. Or, just imagine a bear saying "Cuma here!" to you.

meaningMnemonic: Your mouth is wearing a mask so people won't realize you're the one being so boisterous as you eat your miso . If you cover your mouth with this mask, no one will know you're such a boisterous eater of miso. Hints Okay, this kanji doesn't actually mean "miso," it just means "boisterous." But you'll pretty much only ever see it in the word for miso, so I figured I'd sneak it in here to prepare you for that… Thank me later.
readingMnemonic: You're being boisterous and having your miso outside when suddenly someone shoves so ap ( そ ) in your mouth. "Even your mask can't hide that boisterous miso-eating. Quiet down and wash your mouth out with that soap!" they yell. Hints Using your boisterous mouth, taste the disgusting soapy soap. The soap bubbles are already filling your mouth and stinging your tongue. This is the punishment for those who eat boisterously.

meaningMnemonic: There is a circumference around someone's hair , as in, you can see a circle drawn around the top of their head. As you examine it closer, and pull at it a bit, you realize that someone has carve d the hair off someone's head! Hints Their hair has literally been carved out of their head, and you discovered it. Of course, the nastiness, the smell, and the feel should be applied to your imagination to make the mnemonic stronger.
readingMnemonic: When you think of all the people who could have done this... all the people who could have carve d out someone's hair, only one person comes to mind, and that is Mrs. Chou ( ちょう ). She's the only person evil enough to do something like this. Hints You can also imagine Mrs. Chou doing the act of carving someone's hair out, but that may just be too much.

meaningMnemonic: Use your fingers to grab some guy's foot and catch him! Touching his foot kind of grosses you out, though, which is why you're just catching him with your fingers rather than your whole hand. Hints You have really strong fingers, so once you catch this guy's foot in your pincer grip, there's no way he's escaping.
readingMnemonic: What made you decide to catch this person? The Torah ( とら ). It was written in the Torah that you needed to catch this guy, and you always follow all the Torah's teachings. Hints Your copy of the Torah is pretty unique for having this list of must-catch people. No one else's Torah has this… Have you ever considered you might have a bootleg version?

meaningMnemonic: There’s a tree in your hair , I think it’s a cedar . How did that cedar tree get in your hair? (Certain types of cedar trees have bark that comes off in fine threads, making them very hairy trees. So this kanji makes perfect sense!) Hints Imagine having a cedar tree in your hair. It’s just a little tree, a sapling, but it’s pretty strange and awkward. It does smell nice though. Mmm… cedar.
readingMnemonic: Once the cedar is fully grown, you use the cedar wood to make a guitar for Sue. A Sue gui tar ( すぎ ), if you will. This Sue guitar was made just for Sue. She’ll love it. Hints Give Sue her Sue guitar. Hear Sue squeal with glee as she receives her Sue guitar.

meaningMnemonic: The mouth of the World Tree , all it does is chat and talk . Hints You'd think the World Tree's mouth would talk wisdom, but all it does is chat, chat, chat.
readingMnemonic: To chat or talk with the World Tree, just head over to Sha man Bay ( しゃべ ). Hints The locals shorten Shaman Bay to "Sha Bay," because they always go there to 喋る with the World Tree. Imagine all the shamans hanging about in the bay.

meaningMnemonic: You toss a pair of gold mustache s into your cooking pot and begin simmering them. Some people use bay leaves and whatnot, but where you're from, there's no seasoning you'd rather have in your cooking pot than a couple of gold mustaches. Hints Smell the aromatic vapors as you simmer these gold mustaches in your cooking pot. You can see the gold whiskers slowly melting and turning into a delicious, shimmering broth.
readingMnemonic: Your spouse asks you if they can have a taste of what's in your cooking pot , but you say, " Nah ba be ( なべ ), this is all for me." Hints Undeterred, your spouse keeps trying to sneak a spoon into your cooking pot, but you relentlessly box them out, shouting "Nah, babe" over and over.

meaningMnemonic: Gold is not the same as copper . They are two different metals. Gold is not the same as copper. Hints Take a piece of gold in one hand and a piece of copper in the other. Bang them together furiously as you shout. “GOLD IS NOT THE SAME AS COPPER! GOLD IS NOT THE SAME AS COPPER!”
readingMnemonic: Smashing the copper against the gold has made you tired. You should eat a dou ghnut ( どう ). Go get yourself a doughnut. Hints Mmm… doughnuts. Eat the doughnut and taste its yummy flavor as you look at the piece of copper. It’s shiny.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the radical that look like this are exactly the same. They are both cottage . Hints As long as you know the radical cottage, you know the kanji cottage.
readingMnemonic: You got this cottage from a sha man ( しゃ ). In fact, everyone you know got their cottage from a shaman. One day you're just walking in the woods, and the next thing you know, a shaman is giving you the keys to their old cottage. Hints I guess shamans are moving out a lot around here. Why don't you go look for a cottage you can buy from a shaman! I bet you'll get a pretty good, totally not cursed, deal!

meaningMnemonic: Tsunami s love to slam into valuable things and crush them into oblivion. A tsunami will crush your house and squash your car and never even think to say sorry about it. Hints Imagine looking on in horror as a tsunami surges in and crushes all your most valuable possessions. The despair is absolutely… crushing.
readingMnemonic: A tsunami can crush a house or a car as though it's a tube ( つぶ ) of toothpaste. Hints Think about how easy it would be for you to squash a tube of toothpaste. That's how easy it is for a tsunami to crush your all valuable stuff.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami hits the greenhouse , destroying the last remaining plant life in the area. The tsunami recedes, and there is nothing but sand, and the lands become a desert . Hints The greenhouse was your only hope in turning the desert into a green forest. Now it's all washed away by salt water, meaning nothing will grow anyways. Feel disappointed about this.
readingMnemonic: See the sun come up over the desert , then go back ( ばく ) down. Up, back down, back up, back down. You stand here for days watching because you're so depressed. Stop being so vague in your approach, sun! You’re weirding everyone out! Hints Up, back down, back up, back down. Move your head up and down to keep up with the sun’s movements. Will it ever rise like normal?

meaningMnemonic: You have an alcohol nine times stronger than any other drink, in a bottle shaped like a cross , and you drink it all and become drunk . You're like, so drunk right now from all that alcohol. Nine times more drunk than ever before. Hints Feel how drunk you are as you look at the cross shaped bottle that once held the alcohol. See the cross start to blur in front of you from how drunk you are.
readingMnemonic: Everything's spinning now, you're so drunk it feels like you're on a swi ng ( すい ). Lurching back and forth in your drunkenness, feeling more and more nauseated by all this horrible swinging. Ugh. Hints Imagine that vertigo that comes over you if you lean your head back when you're drunk. It feels like leaning back on a playground swing, in a way. Oh, wait… what if we got drunk and swung on the playground swings? Double swing effect! Actually, never mind. Bad idea.

meaningMnemonic: Fire , fire , flame ! There’s flames everywhere! Hints Feel the fire all around you, the flames licking at your body. It’s really hot!
readingMnemonic: The flame s gets bigger, surround you, and then everything en ds ( えん ). Hints Sorry, but standing in a blaze isn't the best idea. Flames are pretty efficient at ending the lives of the things in it. Maybe you should do this kanji lesson over and try not to stand in the flames next time.

meaningMnemonic: Your car is dry because you kept it under the eaves of your house. This kanji has a second meaning too: house counter . Imagine counting all the houses on your block by the number of eaves you see keeping cars dry. Hints One eave, one house. Two eaves, two houses.
readingMnemonic: On top of the eaves of your house Ken ( けん ) the samurai is counting houses too. Hints Ken hops down and explains that he's been hired to count all the houses in his lord's domain just because his name is the same as the counter for houses. It isn't really fair, he complains to you, as you try to sneak by and lock him out of your house.

meaningMnemonic: You create a thread with someone by call ing out to them to introduce yourself. Hints You literally call out, and when they turn around, tie a thread to them, so you'll never forget that you introduced yourselves to each other.
readingMnemonic: You want to introduce yourself to the Shou gun ( しょう ) but no matter how much you call out, he won't come close enough for you to tie your introduction thread to him. You call louder and louder, "SHOUGUN LET ME INTRODUCE MYSELF!" Hints Finally the Shougun sighs and turns toward you. You call out your name and get the thread around him. Uh oh. He doesn't look happy.

meaningMnemonic: The jammed in radical and the jammed in kanji are the same! Hints Know your radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: Look down! You're jammed in to something. You can't move your feet. What is this?! Oh, your body's been jammed in a kay ak ( かい ). Hints Picture yourself jammed into a kayak. Your pants are bunching and sticking out the sides and top. You really don't fit in here.

meaningMnemonic: The tsunami s during the old moon s (many moons ago) were responsible for the world's lake s. Hints Where did lakes come from? They are the residue of tsunamis from many moons ago.
readingMnemonic: "That's where lake s come from," you tell the 子 ( こ ). Hints This is just a stupid story to get this 子 to stop asking "why, why, why?" about everything. Earlier, the 子 asked "where do lakes come from?" and you had to come up with a crazy story to quiet them.

meaningMnemonic: Try to say something to a lifeguard and you'll just end up getting a lecture . Hints A lifeguard's favorite part of the job is telling people what to do, where to swim, when to get out of the water, and they love saying it in a bunch of words.
readingMnemonic: This lecture loving lifeguard is none other than こう いち ! I mean, look how long winded the stuff on this site is? Can you imagine him trying to give you a talk about proper swimming etiquette? Hints Close your eyes and picture こういち lecturing you. Ugh, it's the worst! Hint: when you see the "lifeguard" radical, the reading is probably going to be こう .

meaningMnemonic: In spring , your measurement s will reveal your lifespan . Only in spring can you measure your lifespan, just as easily as you measure your height and weight. Hints On the first day of spring, all the girls and boys line up to measure their lifespans.
readingMnemonic: If your lifespan measurement isn't as long as you'd like, you need to drink more small ju ice ( じゅ ) boxes this year. They're good for your health, after all! Hints Look at Salmon, over here. She drank a thousand small juice boxes last year and now her measurement says she's gonna live another hundred years!

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami will pick up a bunch of shellfish and dump them on your shore, so you take a knife and measure them. Hints You can't eat shellfish that are too small, so you place your knife along them to measure them. If they're big enough, you stick the knife in and eat them raw.
readingMnemonic: All of the shellfish you measure that are too small go into your sock ( そく ). Once the sock is full, you swing it around your head and lob it back into the ocean. Hints If you measure one of these shellfish and it's too small, stuff it right into your sock. Then once the sock measures about 12 shellfish long, toss it back to sea!

meaningMnemonic: If you're on the edge of a cliff with a snake , that's a misfortune . You're hanging off the edge of this cliff and you can't pull yourself back up. Then you notice a snake approaching your fingers, looking like it's gonna bite you. What a misfortune! Hints What will you do? You can either let go and fall off the cliff, or hold on and get bitten by the snake. Man, talk about misfortune.
readingMnemonic: You decide to let go, but at the bottom of the cliff is an even greater misfortune : yak ( やく ). A whole stampeding herd of yak is passing just as you fall. Oops! You've accidentally committed yourself to the ultimate misfortune, death by yak trampling. Hints Imagine the glittering maze of hooves and yak horns that enclose you now. Ahhh! Then the yak pass, and you find yourself alive but beaten. Life is one misfortune after another, but misfortunes, like the yak, eventually pass…

meaningMnemonic: The ground and a shuriken have mutual respect for one another. The shuriken respects the ground because of how solid and stable it is, and the ground respects the shuriken for how pointy it is. They have great mutual respect here. Hints Pick up the shuriken and throw it into the ground. Hear it whizz through the air and then plunk into the ground. This act of aggression causes their mutual respect to waver.
readingMnemonic: Since you made the shuriken attack the ground, the mutual respect is out of balance. This summons Go dzilla ( ご ) up from the depths of the ocean once more. He always shows up when something is out of wack, to show humans the error of their ways. He picks up the shuriken and flings it into a city, which explodes, leaving a crater in the ground. Hints You give Godzilla a thumbs up, you see what he's trying to do. He looks down at you and nods. Now you have a mutual respect for one another too.

meaningMnemonic: This tsunami is the reason we have so much oil now. The tsunami moved a bunch of earth out of the way, so now it’s really easy to dig for oil. Thanks tsunami! Hints Watch as this tsunami crashes over the land, pushing earth out of the way. Once the tsunami passes, hear the spewing geysers of oil as they erupt out of the ground.
readingMnemonic: Now that oil is so abundant, everyone lives in yu rts ( ゆ ). They're light and mobile, so people can just move from oil well to oil well, collecting oil. Hints Look at how this oil has changed the world. Instead of living in big homes, condos, or skyscrapers, everyone lives in a yurt at night and travels with all the oil by day.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for oneself first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means oneself as well. Hints Make sure you know those radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: Oneself . Who only thinks of oneself? Every 子 ( こ ) in the world. Hints Kids can only think of oneself. Until a certain age, that's literally all they can care about.

meaningMnemonic: You have an animal and you say it’s a dog to prevent it from going to prison . Dogs are the only animals that don’t have to go to prison. Your animal is not a dog, but you say it is to prevent it from going to prison. Hints Imagine any animal that’s not a dog. Now imagine dressing it up like a dog so it doesn’t have to go to prison. Practice throwing your voice by saying “woof woof” aloud to help convince people that your animal is actually a dog.
readingMnemonic: What is the name of your animal? Your animal is named Goku ( ごく ). Yeah, like Goku from Dragon Ball Z. You don’t want your little Goku to go to prison , so you say that he’s a dog. Hints Poor little Goku doesn’t want to go to prison either so Goku does his best to act like a dog even though he isn’t. How adorable.

meaningMnemonic: There's a slide with a drunkard above it, and they're making you feel small . And the worst part is that the drunkard is one of your relatives . Hints A slide isn't the safest place for a drunkard to be. You try to help your relative down but they just keep shouting at you and making you feel small. Drunk relatives are the worst.
readingMnemonic: As if things couldn't get worse, your relative seems to think they're sexy ( せき ) when they're on the slide drunk. Sexy? More like irresponsible! Hints Imagine your intoxicated relative shouting about how sexy they are on that slide. Someone get them down from there!

meaningMnemonic: The sake radical and the sake kanji are exactly the same! Sweet. Hints For goodness sake! Please remember this isn't "sake" as in お酒 ! It's the English "sake," that rhymes with "bake," "cake," and "steak." Oops.. now I'm hungry.
readingMnemonic: For the sake of convenience, companies will use ea gles ( い ) for delivery jobs in the future. Just put in an order, and it'll be at your doorstep in no time flat. Eagles are like, super fast at delivery. Hints See this eagle as it comes to deliver your order just for your sake. Scree! Hear its wings flap and your package plop down on your porch as it's delivered.

meaningMnemonic: Try not to let your mouth get droopy — you'll dribble saliva everywhere. Hints If you feel spit starting to dribble down your chin, it probably means you've let your mouth get all droopy again. Come on — flex those face muscles and get it together!
readingMnemonic: If you need an outlet for all your extra saliva , try playing the tuba ( つば ). A tuba's even got a nifty little spit valve at the bottom, so you can fill it with saliva to your heart's content and then drain it all out when you're done. Hints Imagine opening the spit valve of your tuba and watching a torrent of saliva pour out of it. This is the price you pay for those mellow brassy tones.

meaningMnemonic: Your ear listens to your heart and feels shame . Your heart is full of shame for how you’ve lived your life and when your ear hears all the things you’ve done, your ear feels shame too. Hints Feel the shame. Feel the shame in both your ear and your heart. Imagine the things you’ve done to make you feel so much shame.
readingMnemonic: You must cleanse your spirit of this shame . You decide to complete Hajj ( はじ ) — you know, the Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca. However, when you get there, all the other pilgrims look at you and say, " Hah ( は )! You? You're a lost cause, buddy." It seems even Hajj can't save you from your shame. Hints Hah! What a fool you were to think you could erase your shameful past with a half-hearted attempt at the Hajj. Shame on you.

meaningMnemonic: Next to the scooter , there's a flag warning you that there are sheep around here, so you should go slow . That means you might be late , but at least the sheep will be okay! Hints It's also a warning to the sheep that if they want to ride scooters they should also slow down, because as we all know, sheep are speed demons.
readingMnemonic: You follow the flag, but the sheep refuse to slow down so you have to get creative. You place chee se ( ち ) every ten feet or so, that way the sheep slow down to bend down on their scooters and take a bite. Hints Picture all of the sheep finally going slowly because there is yummy cheese all over the road.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami carries a cross into your soup . Hey tsunami, I was eating that soup! Hints Picture a bowl of soup, but now there is a cross and some tsunami water in it.
readingMnemonic: You pull the cross out of your soup and see that the cross' jew els ( じゅう ) fell off and are in there now. The jewels sparkle, shine, and dissolve into the soup! Hints You're curious so you take a sip of this jewel soup and... it's delicious! You should make more and sell it!

meaningMnemonic: The commander 's alcohol is really just soy sauce . When he goes out to drink with his troops and they all get drunk together, he manages to have fun and stay sober by drinking down a tasty, non-alcoholic pint of soy sauce. Hints The next time you go to a bar, order yourself a commander's alcohol. It's like saying you want a Roy Rogers or a Shirley Temple, except it isn't pretty and it tastes horrible.
readingMnemonic: Soy sauce also happens to be the Shou gun's ( しょう ) favorite drink. Unfortunately, he can't just tell people he likes drinking glasses of soy sauce, or they'll look at him weird. Instead he orders it as a commander's alcohol too. Hints Picture the Shougun sitting on his throne, guzzling down some salty, brown soy sauce. It's splashing on his robes and the smell is making his assistants gag.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami , once stopped by a belt , will begin to stagnate . This belt is a belt of water resistance, so the belt stops the tsunami. The belt has caused the tsunami to stagnate. Hints Watch this belt as it stagnated the tsunami. See the belt glow as its enchantment activates, immediately stagnating the tsunami water.
readingMnemonic: While you watch the tsunami stagnate , you get ready for work. While you were watching this whole thing happening, you were tying your tie ( たい ). Once the tsunami stagnated, you were all done tying your tie. And since the tsunami is no longer a threat, you’re ready to go to work. Hints Look in the mirror at you in your tie. Put the finishing touches on your outfit and imagine going out into the world with your tie on, no longer afraid of any tsunamis. They’re all stagnant now thanks to that magical belt.

meaningMnemonic: Tie a squid to a knife and you get a sword ! Knives are too small to be considered a sword on their own. That's why you strapped a squid to it. They're the right shape, kinda pointed, so no one will know it's just a knife. Hints Imagine creating your own sword out of a knife and a squid.
readingMnemonic: You learned how to make sword s this way from Ken ( けん ) the samurai. He put his own little squid buddy on his knife and now no one realizes it's not a sword! Hints Picture Ken swinging his squid sword at you. *Squish* it squirts ink on your shoulder. But it doesn't really hurt.

meaningMnemonic: If you scrape a sharp stone against your skin , it will tear . The sharp stone tears your skin. It hurts! Hints Imagine this sharp stone. Feel its weight in your hand. Now drag the sharp stone against your skin. Feel your skin as it begins to tear. The pain is agonizing.
readingMnemonic: The moment your skin tear s you can't help but yelp, " Hah ( は )!" It sounds like a laugh, but it's more like a pained bark. Hints You make this noise when you tear other things with the sharp stone too, but now it's more like, "Hah! Take that! Feel the same pain I feel!"

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami goes through a little door , and plops down a big drop on your face. This tsunami is your tears inside your eye area. The door is your tear duct. The big drop is the teardrop coming down your eye. Hints Imagine a teardrop going through this process to get out of your eye, though in a more miniature teardrop size.
readingMnemonic: Your teardrop s are like little waves. What are they? They're 波だ ( なみだ ). Hints Feel each teardrop rolling like a little wave down your cheek. You've never paid such close attention to them before. Teardrops really are just 波だ , you think. Little, ticklish waves.

meaningMnemonic: The turtle radical and the turtle kanji are exactly the same! Nice!
readingMnemonic: You know Dragon Ball Z, right? Imagine this turtle doing a Kame hameha ( かめ ). The turtle charges up his energy and releases a mighty Kamehameha blast. Shwooom! Hints See this turtle as he gathers energy, shaking the earth around him, gathering chi for his Kamehameha blast. He releases it in a mighty blast of energy. Kamehameha!!

meaningMnemonic: To make alcohol the key is to ferment it. But, if you ferment it a certain way, it will become vinegar . Hints Imagine making a bunch of vinegar. You use a key to change it from alcohol to vinegar, yum!
readingMnemonic: You are demonstrating this practice in front of an audience. You want them to take you seriously so you wear a su it ( す ). A very nice suit. Surely they will now believe that you can turn alcohol into vinegar . Hints Imagine yourself doing the same thing as before but you are now wearing a suit. Dang, you look good.

meaningMnemonic: When something is slight , that means you only have a few or a little of that thing. 僅か is a relatively formal word that indicates a small amount. You'll hear it when someone wants to emphasize how little something is, like 僅かな差 (a little gap) or 僅か10分 ( just ten minutes). Note this word is often written in kana, as わずか , unless the writing style is very formal.
readingMnemonic: When people have just a few of something, wars ( わず ) tend to break out. So many wars have started because there was only a little of something and people began to fight over it.

sentences.english: Only a tiny handful of people can do something like that.

meaningMnemonic: Two people's efforts mix in a mutual way when they work alternately . Going by turns is not only fair — it's efficient too! 交互に is a relatively formal adverb that describes two things occurring in alternating succession — whether that's a pair of visual elements repeating alternately in a pattern, or just two people taking turns doing something, one after the other .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.english: to do alternately, to alternate

sentences.english: to alternate between eating

sentences.english: Let's take turns reading pages.

sentences.english: Since there was only one controller, I told them to take turns playing.

sentences.english: She alternated between licking two different flavors of ice cream.

sentences.japanese: このボタンを押すと、二つのプログラムが交互に実行されます。
sentences.english: When you press this button, the two programs are executed alternately.

meaningMnemonic: You've got a very element al person . They're so elementary that they're quite an amateur , really. Maybe a little too elemental.
readingMnemonic: Unfortunately, the reading for this is a complete exception, so you'll just have to memorize it. Here's a mnemonic to help you: "You're an amateur !", she wrote ( しろうと ). A little harsh, isn't it? But that's what she wrote. Gotta do a little better to impress her, pal.

sentences.japanese: ど素人
sentences.english: a complete novice

sentences.japanese: 素人レベル

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. meaningMnemonic: Remember how 儲ける means "to make a profit"? Well, this is the intransitive version — the version that doesn't take a direct object — so it means to be profitable . Compared to 儲ける , which is about you gaining something, 儲かる is more about the situation itself bringing in money, like この店は儲かってる (this shop is doing well). It can also refer to some benefit coming in by luck, like 一日儲かった (I got an extra day).

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You learned this kanji means "model," but it can also mean " take into account ," so the verb version means to take something into account or to be in light of . 鑑みる literally comes from the idea of "looking at something closely to judge it." It's a formal word used to describe the act of thoughtfully considering something based on things like prior experiences or surrounding circumstances. It's a transitive verb, but it can take を or に to mark the thing you're taking into account. Both particles are grammatically correct, but に sounds slightly more formal, which often matches the contexts where this word is used.
readingMnemonic: This verb uses the kun'yomi of the kanji. You haven't learned that yet, so here's mnemonic to help you: If you want to take something into account , you'll need to 考 える ( かんが ) about it really hard first. And when you do that thinking, it has to be in light of lots of other factors. Taking all those factors into account will help guide your next move, you know?
